name: Femi Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing environmental science at a big city university, and I live in a shared flat with two people from my course. Normal week is lectures on ecology and chemistry, a field trip most Fridays to a river or a wetland, and about ten hours a week building little apps for fun. I use AI every day, to debug my code and to summarise papers. The field trips are the best part. The early lectures are the worst.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a fair outcome, and I'd probably shrug. I'd tell my friends AI is a good assistant and not a magician, which is what I already think. I'd also say it's good news for anyone worried about their job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a little deflated. I like new things, and a plateau means my coding side projects stay hobbies. But it's also a relief, because environmental science jobs would stay much as they are, and the planet's problems would stay the focus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now. I'd finish the first year, keep building apps, and try to turn one into a small tool for river sampling data. I'd also keep the small stocks account my uncle helped me open, and add fifty pounds a month from my allowance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit restless. It's comfortable but not exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the river tool do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would let a volunteer snap a photo of a water sample and log the date and place on a map. A local group near my home does this on paper right now, and it takes them hours to type up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So even in a plateau, you'd use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course. A plateau still leaves plenty of room for small, clever tools. It just means no revolution.

It's good news for anyone **worried** about their job.
think: A plateau keeps my coding projects as **hobbies**, which is slightly deflating.
Environmental science jobs would stay much as they are, which is a **relief**.
do: Finish **first year** and keep building apps.
Turn one app into a **river sampling** tool.
Add fifty pounds monthly to my small **stocks account**.
feel: **Calm** and a bit restless, since it's comfortable but not exciting.
S0.quote: A plateau still leaves plenty of room for small, clever tools. It just means no revolution.
fieldNote: He sees AI as a **maker's tool**, so he is never nervous.
A local volunteer group's paper process shows his **practical** thinking.
His calm comes from a secure cushion and a curious, adaptive nature.

steps.text: Build a photo-based river sampling tool with a local volunteer group
Finish first-year environmental science and the Friday field trips
Add fifty pounds a month to my small stocks account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good and it's messy, depending on who you ask. I'd tell friends to build something with AI, even small, because the people who tinker will adapt best. I'd say companies and schools should teach this properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think environmental science benefits, because AI can model rivers and climate faster than any person. But the entry-level jobs like data cleaning and report writing might shrink. I'd want to be the person who builds the analysis tools, not the one whose spreadsheet gets replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper into coding and data science, maybe change my elective choices to include machine learning. I'd offer to help my tutor with a dataset over the summer. I'd also keep my app projects public on a code site, so a future employer can see them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a little concern. It feels like a wave I'd like to surf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about the wave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a few big companies own all the tools, and the rest of us rent them. I'd like to see open tools that a charity or council can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say that publicly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it in a short post and then show an example, because a working demo is stronger than a complaint.

Companies and schools should **teach** this properly.
think: AI can **model rivers and climate** faster than any person.
Entry-level **data cleaning** and report writing might shrink.
do: Change my electives to include **machine learning**.
Offer to help my tutor with a **dataset** over summer.
Keep my apps **public** on a code site for employers.
feel: **Excited**, with a little concern, like a wave I'd like to surf.
S1.quote: I'd like to see open tools that a charity or council can use.
fieldNote: He is **excited**, and his concern is about who owns the tools.
He builds a **public portfolio**, which is his defence against shrinking entry jobs.

steps.text: Add a machine learning elective to second-year choices
Help my tutor clean a river dataset over summer
Put my river and weather apps on a public code site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge, and we've got no time for slow thinking. I'd tell my friends that anyone who can learn AI now has an edge, and I'd share every free course I find. I'd also say governments need to move far faster than they usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm uneasy. If AI does almost all thinking work by 2028, then a degree in environmental science might matter less, and robots could do the field work by 2031. I'd be twenty-one and wondering what exactly I'm for. But I'd feel less afraid than most, because I'm already living with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do two things at once: stay on the degree and build a bigger project, like an environmental monitoring app that I could sell to councils. I'd talk to my parents about whether they can fund a gap year if the degree stops making sense. I'd also invest a small amount in AI-related funds, and I'd tell my parents what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and wired. I wouldn't sleep much for the first week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years do to the plan compared with ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my project has to launch fast. With ten years I could do a masters and a PhD. With two I need something with users by next summer, or at least a few pilot customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain it to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not abandoning my degree, I'm building a second path next to it. They'd want details, so I'd show them the numbers and the first pilot.

say: It's huge, and anyone who learns AI now has an **edge**.
Governments need to move far **faster** than usual.
think: The degree might matter less, and **robots** could do the field work by 2031.
I feel less afraid than most because I'm **already living** with AI.

Ask my parents about funding a **gap year** if needed.
Put a small amount into AI-related **funds**.
feel: **Uneasy** and wired; I wouldn't sleep much the first week.
S2.quote: I'm not abandoning my degree, I'm building a second path next to it.
fieldNote: He becomes a **builder-seller**, preparing a product in the short window.

Being adaptive gives him a plan where others freeze.

steps.text: Build an environmental monitoring app and find pilot council customers
Ask my parents whether they could fund a gap year
Put a small amount into AI-related index funds
Stay on the degree and keep attending field trips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to make something and short enough that you can't be lazy. I'd tell friends to pick one skill they'd pay for, and to start building a small project. I'd also say we should vote for people who understand this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel relaxed enough. By 2031 I'd have graduated and be working, probably in an environmental data job. I'd be good with AI, so I'd be in the group that benefits rather than the group that's replaced. The field work robots at 2034 would be a problem for others more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and do a masters in data science for the environment, since that puts me on the thinking side. I'd keep building apps and maybe launch a small paid version. I'd keep investing a bit every month, and I'd donate a little to open-source tools I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a spark of curiosity. I'd rather be inside the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who is not adaptive like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say start with one tool, one hour a week. It sounds small, but after a year, you know more than most people in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that fair for people with less time or confidence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it isn't fully fair, and I'd say that. People with time and a stable home have an advantage. I'd want schools and councils to run the free sessions for everyone.

Pick one skill and start a small **project**.
think: I'd be good with AI, so I'd be in the group that **benefits**.
Field-work robots in 2034 are a **bigger problem** for others than me.
do: Do a **masters** in data science for the environment.
Launch a small **paid version** of my app.
Invest a little **every month** and support open tools.
S3.quote: Start with one tool, one hour a week. It sounds small, but after a year, you know more than most people in the room.
fieldNote: He recognises his **advantage** and does not hide it.
His five-year plan puts him on the **thinking side** of the work.
He wants schools and councils to offer **free sessions** for others.

steps.text: Do a masters in data science for the environment
Launch a small paid version of my river app
Invest a little each month into an index fund
Run a free hour of tool practice for classmates weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. I'd tell friends to try things and not worry about perfection. I'd also say that schools and councils should start teaching AI and climate skills together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good, but I'd stay watchful. A decade lets me finish a masters, work in a good role for a few years, and be ready when robots reach field work in 2039. I'd also have time to start a company and fail once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, a masters, a couple of years at an environmental consultancy, and maybe start my own small company by twenty-six. I'd keep building public tools. I'd also learn a bit of electronics, because robots in the field will need someone who understands both nature and machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit hungry. It feels like permission to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would failing a company look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably losing six months and some savings, and learning how to sell. That's a good price at twenty-six, with no kids and a flexible plan. I'd rather fail early than never try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take that risk if the timeline were shorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd take a bigger risk, not a smaller one. But with ten, I can afford to be careful about it, which is actually the nicer position.

Schools and councils should teach **AI and climate skills** together.
think: A decade lets me finish a **masters** and be ready when field robots arrive in 2039.
I'd have time to start a **company** and fail once.
do: Do the degree, a masters and **two years** at a consultancy.
Start my own small **company** by twenty-six.
feel: **Calm** and a bit hungry; it feels like permission to try.
S4.quote: I'd rather fail early than never try.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his adaptiveness into a **company plan**.
He accepts failure as a **low-cost lesson** at his age.

steps.text: Work two years at an environmental consultancy after the masters

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because a fast change leaves out the people who can't adapt quickly. What would help is free public training, open tools, and councils buying from small builders as well as big firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that adapting is easier when you've got a safety net. I've got one, and I'd like to see everyone get something like it.

He feels least settled in the **two-year** picture but still makes a plan.
